Search found no single "fastest" algorithm — it's workload-dependent: introsort/quicksort usually wins on random in-memory comparison data, Timsort wins on partially sorted data, and radix wins on large fixed-width integer keys. I put that to the test in Python.

What I wrote and ran — /Users/a1-6/Mypro/genai/GenAI2OpenAI/temp/claude-workflow-3na7jjfu/benchmark.py: a pure-Python introsort (quicksort with median-of-three pivot, insertion sort under 16 elements, heapsort fallback on deep recursion), compared against CPython's sorted() (Timsort, C-implemented) on six defined 20k-element inputs plus a 1k input, and edge cases (empty, single, all-equal, reversed, random 500). All correctness assertions passed and the script printed SORT_BENCH_OK.

Measured (Python 3.11.14, best of 3 runs):
| input | introsort | sorted() | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| random | 11.093 ms | 1.689 ms | 6.6x |
| sorted | 6.155 ms | 0.106 ms | 58.0x |
| reversed | 6.390 ms | 0.090 ms | 71.1x |
| many_duplicates | 8.782 ms | 1.191 ms | 7.4x |
| nearly_sorted | 6.315 ms | 0.205 ms | 30.8x |
| small_1000 | 0.373 ms | 0.050 ms | 7.5x |

Conclusion: algorithmically, introsort is the fastest comparison sort on random data and Timsort dominates on sorted/reversed/nearly-sorted data. But in Python, sorted() beat introsort on every input (6.6x–71x) because it's C-level hybrid Timsort versus interpreted Python bytecode — so the practical quickest sort in Python is the built-in sorted().
